item.title: SALES: The Comfortable Sneakers Our Editors Have Traveled the World In
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
A comfortable pair of sneakers is the most essential part of my travel uniform—after all, it doesn't matter how cute my loungewear set is if my feet are covered in blisters. The best sneakers conquer those 20,000-step-days without missing a beat, whether I'm racing to my gate at the airport, rolling heavy luggage down cobblestone streets, or exploring a new city by foot. And they look good too: My favorite sneakers to travel in are on-trend and versatile enough to wear with multiple outfits. My fellow Traveler editors agree: We've walked through New York City, Paris, Tokyo, and beyond wearing our go-to pairs, trusting them to keep up with our every move. Below, browse through the sneakers we recommend most for long travel days, from Salomon's popular XT-6 to the always-in-style Adidas Sambas. Top picks: The newest addition to my shoe lineup is this fun, suede sneaker from Rothy's, my most-trusted footwear brand for travel. I've been wearing them nonstop the past few months, from pumpkin picking and apple cider donut chasing to strolling through the city and commuting to the office. Most of my everyday sneakers are white and fairly simple looking, whereas these cheetah print shoes add a little flare to any outfit. They're incredibly lightweight while offering enough support and cushioning for a full day on my feet. My favorite thing about them is the incredibly grippy outsole. They remind me of the nonslip shoes I used to wear during my days working at a restaurant—but way, way cuter. I don't worry about slipping in them or missing a step, even when I'm walking on rainy sidewalks in NYC. Once reserved for soccer, the Adidas Samba made a big comeback a few years ago—and we have no plans to stop wearing them. The low-top sporty shoes complete any street style look, all while providing plenty of comfort. Editorial assistant Kat Chen swears by these practically weightless sneakers. “They are my ride or die. I got this newest pair last summer, but the ones I had before I wore for literally a decade until they finally wore down,” says Chen. I'm also a fan; I reach for them when I need something casual and comfy to wear with jeans or trousers. I've even worn them for a full day walking around DC, and most recently, a dance-filled Harry Styles concert at Madison Square Garden without any complaints. Associate editor Charlie Hobbs isn't shy about his long-standing love for New Balance dad shoes. His claim: They are the ultimate travel shoe. Among his favorites are the popular 9060 sneaker. “They are the only sneakers I pack," says Hobbs. “My conservatism is rewarded. I am obsessed with these sneakers and they are so comfortable.” They shine for both style and comfort, and work well year-round. “The shoes don't merely survive such 30,000 step days—they improve, becoming softer, easier to wear, and never staining with the dust of the Tiergarten,” says Hobbs. I know what you're thinking: a platform shoe…for travel? Yes, really. The Gazelle comes highly recommended by several of our editors, especially commerce director Madison Flager who says they were comfortable from the very first wear. They add just a little bit of height (about an inch) without the discomfort of a heeled bootie or sandal. “I’ve put them on for concerts in which I knew I'd be standing for a few hours straight and on a trip with no regrets,” says Flager. “Most recently, they came with me to Nashville on a particularly rainy weekend and stayed in good shape without me having to avoid puddles.” She does recommend sizing down half a size as they run a bit big. Possibly the most iconic shoe on our list, you can't go wrong with a pair of high-top Converse. They've been around for more than a century, loved by athletes and travelers everywhere, including senior commerce editor Hannah Chubb, who wore them to the US Open this past summer. “I've owned my fair share of white Converse over the years—low-tops in high school, high-tops post-college—because they're just so darn classic,” she says. “They never go out of style, add a little tomboy flair to any outfit, and keep my feet happy no matter how many miles I put on them.” Despite their low profile, these lightweight Adidas offer an impressive amount of support. They carried associate social media manager Pooja Nayyar through a two-week Euro trip this summer—cobblestone streets and all! They've quickly become her go-to pair for everyday wear too. “Not only do they match every outfit, but they are extremely comfortable,” says Nayyar. “And as a pleasant surprise, they didn’t get destroyed when I got caught in a rainstorm.” I've been wearing these New Balance 574s for over four years. They're a perfect balance of practical and cute, and are neutral enough to match nearly anything in my carry-on. Looks aside, they are extremely comfortable. From long commutes to the office to city walking tours around Boston, they've kept my feet comfortable every time. What stands out most to me is how lightweight they are—despite giving off the cool dad shoe vibe, they aren't clunky or heavy at all. They've also stayed in excellent condition over the years, which is more than I can say about most of my white sneakers. If you're looking for a polished white sneaker that can work with multiple outfits in your suitcase, this pair from Atoms has you covered. “I admit, I have a lot of white sneakers in my closet, but these are the ones I take out the most, whether I'm walking around New York City or packing for a trip,” says Flager, who has had this pair for over two years. “They're super lightweight, comfortable, and have never given me any blisters or irritation, even when I'm wearing no-show socks. As bright white shoes, they do get scuffed fairly easily, but I've been able to keep them looking new by spot-cleaning with laundry detergent.” For something a little more fun than your everyday white sneaker, this pair from Onitsuka Tiger is a nice addition to your closet—and they're just as comfy as they are cool. Senior features editor Megan Spurrell regularly travels with them in her suitcase. “They have a super low profile but still offer great arch support,” she says. Best of all: “They always remind me of being in Japan.” Alo's Sunset Sneaker is another pair of comfortable daytime shoes I reach for often. They are practically weightless on my feet and the low profile gives them an effortlessly cool look. The neutral colorway makes them versatile, while the 100% suede material looks super polished. I've worn these with low-rise jeans, trousers, skirts, and even exercise dresses thanks to their sporty look. And because they're so lightweight, I've been able to pack them in my carry-on without much added bulk. Commerce writer Jessica Chapel swears by this pair from Adidas. “I've always been an Adidas girl—whether it be the OG Stan Smith's or this fun, newer take on an old classic,” says Chapel. “I slip them on to run to the grocery store, walk to the park, or brunch all around town. They're the definition of practical: Even when they get dirty, the outer material makes it easy to clean off with a damp towel.” Salomon sneakers are having a moment; you've probably seen them everywhere from coffee shops to hiking trails. The popular XT-6 is durable enough for an active day and chic enough to elevate your travel ’fit. Commerce writer Jessica Sulima has had her trusty Salomons for more than four years. “I love wearing them to the airport because I don’t have to worry about frantically untying laces at security; the Quicklace closure allows you to slip them on and off with ease,” she says. “I’ve brought them on every kind of trip, from hiking excursions (ankle support) to city romps (gorp-core chic), and they do equally as well wherever they go.” If you need something study and supportive for rugged adventures, Alo's sleek Trail Sneaker is a safe bet. The brand is known and loved for its activewear, but its sneakers deserve some hype too. Commerce producer ElleAnna Revell recommends them for morning walks and long hikes. “They are super flexible and comfortable while still being very durable,” says Revell. “I have them in black, and they are so easy to style and go with absolutely everything.” The sneaker that completes my in-flight uniform every single time is this pair of Hoka Cliftons. I fly in them, I work out in them, I go on walks in them—I trust these shoes with my life. They're the only athletic pair of sneakers I pack on every trip. They have what looks like a thick platform, and that extra cushion and shock absorption only adds to the shoe’s comfort level. The EVA foam midsole provides a ton of support and makes your feet feel like they're on a pillow. I've had them for over two years and they are easily my most-worn shoe. You probably know On for its best-selling running shoes, but they're great for busy travel days too. “As a blister girlie that’s also quite fashion-conscious, I’m very picky about my sneakers,” says Chubb. “On’s Cloud 6 sneakers have been my go-to on recent travels because they feel light as air, don’t rub on my heels (I swear every shoe does this to me), match with all my athleisure fits, and are easy to slip on and off at the airport thanks to the bungee laces.” This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: REVIEW: Edifier Hecate G2000 Pro Review: Clear and Colorful
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
A unique-looking set of RGB-laden speakers that offers an impressive soundstage as well as multi-source connectivity options. - -The clear speaker enclosure and RGB aren’t for everyone's tastes - -Finicky double-presses of buttons needed for switching between lighting modes and stored audio EQ Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Why settle for ordinary when you can spice up your gaming setup with a pair of unique-looking RGB-laden desktop PC speakers? Edifier’s Hecate G2000 Pro speakers instantly stand out in both looks and sound, with the small desktop 2.0 speakers outputting a much larger soundstage than their size would have you believe. These versatile speakers are enjoyable for both gaming and music listening, and offer good value with plenty of connectivity options. The design of the Edifier Hecate G2000 Pro 2.0 system has a different speaker design that I haven't really seen before: A squished and elongated hexagonal shape, with a clear, see-through speaker enclosure and bright RGB lighting. They look unique and modern, maybe even a little futuristic — and while I’m not a fan of the overuse of RGB lighting in general, I like them. (You can also easily turn the lighting off, so you aren’t left stuck with distracting flashing lights 24/7.) Both speakers aim the sound toward your ears with a 10° tilted angle built into the shape of the speaker, so there's no need for any angled desktop speaker pads or stands. The right speaker contains all the tech, with controls on the top of the speaker — four rubberized silicone buttons — and power and connectivity options on the rear. The two speakers are connected by a hardwired 1.5-meter braided cord, which is plenty of length for most desk sizes. Large rubber feet on the bottom of the speakers soothe vibrations and stop the speakers from slipping around the space. The speakers are solidly built and feel very sturdy and weighty when you hold them. On the rear of the speakers is the opening for the bass reflex port, a clear port that you can see inside the transparent speaker enclosure, and complete with a little mesh dust filter midway along the port to keep the inside of the enclosure clean. Performance of the Edifier Hecate G2000 Pro I put the Edifier Hecate G2000 Pro speakers through their paces, testing them while gaming and listening to lossless audio via my PC and via Bluetooth on my phone. In gaming, the sound is clear and positional audio cues are easy to detect. The 7.1 virtual surround sound is enabled via the Xear software and does some heavy lifting in games that have good positional audio composition; however, in games that have more of a stereo soundscape, the 7.1 just seems to add echo and reverb to the mix, and doesn’t sound good at all. While playing Battlefield 6, I was impressed with the volume and gravitas of the cinematic explosions and sound of crumbling infrastructure, with individual sounds of gunfire and footsteps easily identifiable in the chaos. My set of Logitech speakers that I usually use on my gaming PC includes a subwoofer, so the bass rumble of explosions is far greater — with the desk and room vibrating when the volume is high. You won’t get that with the Edifier Hecate G2000 Pro, but the rumble is still impressive for a small 2.0 speaker setup, and the clarity and depth of the soundstage are impressive. There is no port for a subwoofer on the G2000 Pro, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing for what are essentially a pair of bedroom PC speakers. Being able to watch a movie or play games without waking up the whole house or even your neighbours gives these speakers a valuable niche, but they still have enough power with 32W total output power to turn up the volume and blast some tunes when the timing is right. You can add some dynamic bass boost via the Xear software, but I found that sound from the speakers without the added bass was far superior, with the default flat EQ offering the best experience. Inside the Hecate G2000 Pro is a single 3-inch speaker driver. It does a great job for just one driver, but not having any separate tweeters or high-frequency speakers means it’s trying to accomplish quite a bit. The overall soundscape suffers slightly because of this, with some muddying at lower volumes — but only slightly. The overall sound is superb for a pair of small mid-range desktop gaming speakers, with an excellent soundstage and big sound not relative to the size of the G2000 Pro. Obviously, they aren’t as bottom-heavy as a 2.1 system with the lack of a dedicated subwoofer, but the bass is still impressive for such small speakers. Features and Software of the Edifier Hecate G2000 Pro One of the best aspects of the Hecate G2000 Pro is the number of connectivity options you have for your audio sources. There’s an AUX port that I used to connect to my sound mixer, a USB-C port for connecting directly to the PC (included USB-C to USB-A cable plus a USB-A to USB-C adapter) via USB-C or USB-A, and also a Bluetooth connection. Although the speakers work flawlessly when connecting via Bluetooth, I did find the source audio wasn’t as clear as it was via the AUX or USB connection. There’s a 3.5mm headphone jack located on the rear if you want to connect a pair of headphones — and you can enable 7.1 surround for the headphones in the Xear software options. The downloadable audio software for the G2000 Pro is very basic. Right-click on the speaker icon for interactive actions, and you can enable/disable the EQ, Dynamic Bass, Audio Brilliant, Smart Volume, and Voice Clarity; there’s also a separate 7.1 surround option for use with headphones through a connection on the speaker. You can also change the lighting without having to use the buttons on the speakers themselves. A volume slider is included, but it's completely unnecessary with the physical buttons on the speakers and various Windows OS volume controls. Most of all, the small selectable UI elements make for a terrible experience; the radial buttons are tiny and an annoyance. I also found that making any changes to the lighting managed to disrupt any music that was playing on Spotify, so there are some software conflicts there. To be honest, you do not need this software at all to use these speakers on a Windows PC, and I could not notice any discernible improvement in sound quality when listening to music. The 7.1 audio in games is okay if the game supports it, but leave it off in a game that doesn’t; the sounds you hear can be pretty terrible. For a mid-range set of speakers at $249 MSRP, the Edifier Hecate G2000 Pros are pretty good. They are an improvement over the Edifier G2000 speakers ($109 MSRP) in power output, driver size, and pretty lighting, but do lack the ability to connect a subwoofer. The sound quality, clarity, and loudness are impressive for the speakers' size, and these speakers sound great even without the added PC software. They are loud enough for any bedroom gaming setup and will appeal to anyone who loves to add a little RGB illumination to their gaming space. The transparent speaker enclosure is novel and looks great, and definitely offers something unique to any battlestation.

item.title: REVIEW: CRKD Nitro Deck 2 review: a great but heavy Switch 2 handheld controller
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The CRKD Nitro Deck 2 is an all-encompassing handheld solution for the Switch and Switch 2, offering a multiplatform controller, backplate protection, and a kickstand all in one unit. There are some ergonomic and minor connectivity issues, but the Nitro Deck 2 is hard to beat if you want the ultimate handheld experience on Nintendo’s platforms. - -Slightly awkward back button placements Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The CRKD Nitro Deck 2 is primarily billed as a Nintendo Switch 2 controller for handheld use, but it offers a lot more besides. It's CRKD’s follow-up to the Nitro Deck and Nitro Deck+, two previous accessories aimed at the original Nintendo Switch. The CRKD Nitro Deck 2 has a functional design focused more on ergonomics than style, although some of the colorways add some panache; the Pal Grey variant I reviewed, for instance, harked back to retro Nintendo controllers, thanks to its colorful face buttons and darker grey accents. The Nitro Deck 2 fits to the Switch and Switch 2 by clamping on the sides of the unit, rather than actually connecting to the Joy-Con 2 slots. A small button on the back clicks and twists to tightly grip your console, and tight it is; even when I held it upside down, my console didn’t move an inch. You can then connect to your console wirelessly via Bluetooth or wired by using the included U-shaped USB adapter. CRKD’s mobile app can be used to remap the inputs of the Nitro Deck 2, as well as enable the ‘No Deadzone’ mode for the joysticks. Its interface is clear and easy to use, and I didn’t experience any bugs. One downside, though, is that you have to reconnect to the app every time you open it by holding two buttons for three seconds, which limits the convenience of back-and-forth adjustments. All the buttons feel great, providing plenty of clicky feedback and responsiveness. The back buttons are awkwardly placed, though, and I found myself accidentally triggering them on occasion. The real highlight of the Nitro Deck 2, though, is its joysticks. Not only are they precise and responsive, but they also feature dials that let you adjust their tension at any point, which is an excellent design choice and should allow any gamer to get their preferred feel. Unfortunately, poor ergonomics detract from the Nitro Deck 2’s otherwise positive performance aspects. Not only do the pads angle inwards at the bottom, contrary to the majority of gamepads, but it’s also heavy when loaded with a console. These factors can make it cumbersome and awkward to use, especially when trying to game upright. The Nitro Deck 2 is easy to pair to the Switch or Switch 2 via Bluetooth, although it takes a while to reconnect to your console after sleeping. Reconnection is quicker in wired mode, but it’s still not instantaneous. It was also easy to pair with PC and Android devices, although it’s a shame you can’t switch between them without having to pair each time. The battery life of the Nitro Deck 2 is reasonable, lasting for as long as CRKD claims (15-20 hours), according to my testing. It’s a small inconvenience that you have to charge it separately from your console, though. When you consider all that it offers, the Nitro Deck 2 represents good value. Not only are you getting handheld pads for the Switch 1 and Switch 2, but you’re also getting protection for your console, a standalone controller you can use with other platforms besides Nintendo’s, and a kickstand. Comfort issues do hamper the experience somewhat, but if you don’t mind holding a weighty unit, the Nitro Deck 2 is a fine choice as a versatile gamepad. CRKD Nitro Deck 2 review: Price & availability - Good price for a versatile handheld gamepad The Nitro Deck 2 costs $89.99 / £89.99 / AU$161 and is available now in four colorways: Smoke Black, Pal Grey, LRG Fusion, and White. It comes with a USB cable, a double-ended USB adapter, and a legacy adapter for Switch 1 compatibility. The joystick caps and D-pad hat are replaceable, but no extra sets for either are included in the box. This is a reasonable price for a unit that’s not only a Switch and Switch 2 handheld case and handheld controller, but also a standalone gamepad for PC and mobile, both wired and wireless. You won’t find many more complete solutions for your Switch 2 than this, or even third-party substitutes for the Joy-Con 2 controllers, save for a few examples, such as the Mobapad M12 HD and M12S. A more left-field alternative to the Nitro Deck 2 is the GameSir G8+, a Bluetooth mobile controller that doesn’t officially support the Switch 2, but users have reported compatibility with the system. If you just want a more comfortable handheld experience for your Switch 2 while sticking with the Joy-Con 2 pads, the Genki Attack Vector is a reasonably priced solution that offers three sets of grips as well as a backplate cover. What’s more, it can remain attached to your console when docked. CRKD Nitro Deck 2 review: Design & features The Nitro Deck 2 has an appearance that’s more about function than form, with its soft edges and curves being more about ergonomics than aesthetics. It’s a fetching piece of design nonetheless, and the Pal Grey finish of my review unit added a retro appeal, with its dark grey accents and colorful face buttons alluding to the classic SNES controller. The build quality is respectable, too. Although the plastic shell didn’t initially strike me as being particularly premium, I quickly felt its solidity and sturdiness once I held it in my hands. The sliding mechanisms for both pads operate smoothly as well. Rather than the pads of the Nitro Deck 2 actually attaching to each Joy-Con slot on the Switch or Switch 2, they simply clamp to the sides of the console without actually inserting into these slots. To tighten the clamp, you simply push and twist the button on the rear of the unit. This requires a fair amount of force, and so does releasing it to remove the console, but I wouldn’t say it was overly arduous, and it’s worth the effort for the secure fit it provides. When attached, the Switch 2 fits snugly and securely; I had no worries about it coming loose, as there wasn’t a hint of looseness. The unit also aligns precisely with the dimensions and contours of the Switch 2, although my one small gripe is that accessing the game card flap can be fiddly, as there’s little room to reach down to lift it up. This isn’t an issue when the Nitro Deck 2 is attached to the Switch 1, though, since the flap on that console opens the other way. Speaking of which, the Nitro Deck 2 fits just as well to the Switch 1 as it does to the Switch 2. Thanks to the included legacy adapter, its USB-C port is still accessible, so you can still have a wired connection between the console and the Nitro Deck 2. This wired connection to both the Switch 1 and 2 is handled by another adapter, a double-ended U-shaped USB-C jack, that slots into the bottom of the Deck and the console. The Nitro Deck 2 also features a kickstand on the back, allowing you to use your console with another controller. This is made of metal and feels very solid. It’s also very sturdy when open, and it folds flush into the back of the Deck. It can be a little difficult to release it from its clip, but this is a small price to pay for its secure fastening. To customize the inputs of the extra shoulder and back buttons, you can use the M button in combination with others to alter the mapping. However, you can also use CRKD’s mobile app, where you can remap every button, as well as enable a ‘No Deadzone’ mode for the joysticks in order to increase their sensitivity. The app is clearly laid out and easy to navigate, and I didn’t experience any bugs or glitches, which was somewhat of a surprise given the poor rating it has on app stores. For some bizarre reason, though, it only operates in landscape mode, but more frustrating is the fact that switching between the app and your console isn’t exactly a seamless experience; you have to hold the Home button and the left D-pad button for 3 seconds every time you go back to the app after exiting it. While its grips may look ergonomic, I struggled to get entirely comfortable with the Nitro Deck 2. Partly, this is due to the sheer weight of the unit when loaded with a console, which makes holding it upright a chore, even for short periods. But the other half of the problem stems from the grips’ orientation. They protrude outwards at the top rather than at the bottom, running counter to the best Nintendo Switch 2 controller shapes, and are at a less natural angle for your hands. I did acclimatize to their form somewhat, but I was never entirely at ease with it. I also found the back buttons awkward to use, as they were too low down to align with my natural finger placement around the grips. Their low travel and resistance meant there were times when I accidentally triggered them, too. These issues aside, though, the Nitro Deck 2 offers fantastic performance. The face buttons are clicky and satisfying to use, while the D-pad is very comfortable thanks to its circular hat. Its floating design also meant presses had plenty of travel, which in turn created good feedback. I found the shoulder buttons were easy to reach and use as well. The best input of all, though, is the joysticks, which feature dials at their bases for adjusting resistance on the fly. This is a great idea and one I wish more controllers implemented. Looser settings allow for easy maneuvering and quick flicks, while tighter settings give you more control and precision. The Nitro Deck 2 also features motion controls. I found these to be accurate and responsive when aiming with the bow in The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, although using them in handheld mode isn’t exactly practical, given the whole console moves with your hands. Unfortunately, I did experience some small connectivity issues with the Nitro Deck 2. Although pairing with my consoles was a relatively quick process, it can be slow to reconnect when you wake your console. It activated quicker when I used a wired connection, but it wasn’t instant. The Nitro Deck 2 worked just as well with my Switch 1 as it did with my Switch 2. It’s a shame, though, that the aforementioned legacy adapter doesn’t support console charging. I’m not sure whether this was a particular issue with my review unit or a known limitation, but either way it’s a shame from a convenience perspective. As for other platforms, I had no issues connecting or using the Nitro Deck 2 with PC or my Android smartphone via Bluetooth, although hot-switching isn’t possible, with pairing required each time you move between devices. The battery life of the Nitro Deck 2 is reasonable — according to my testing, it lasts about as long as CRKD claims it can, which is between 15 and 20 hours. However, it’s a shame you can’t charge your console and the Deck with a single cable, as there’s no passthrough feature. Should I buy the CRKD Nitro Deck 2? With the instantly adjustable tension for the joysticks, every gamer should be able to get the right feel. Not only does the Nitro Deck 2 work with the Switch and Switch 2 in handheld mode, but it can also be used to game on PC and mobile devices. You want something light and very portable With a console attached, the Nitro Deck 2 is noticeably heavy and bulky in the hand. The Nitro Deck 2 doesn’t wake up instantly with your console, and switching between devices requires repairing. Although not explicitly marketed as a Switch 2 controller, user reports suggest that the G8+ does indeed work with the console. When we tested it on mobile devices, we were impressed with its comfortable grips and smooth, precise thumbsticks and triggers. Read our full GameSir G8+ review. If you want to stick with the Joy-Con 2 pads but require better handheld ergonomics, Genki’s accessory may just fit the bill. It comes with three sets of grips to accommodate all kinds of hands, while the back cover adds some protection to your Switch 2 without compromising its fit in the dock (unlike the Nitro Deck 2). Read our full Genki Attack Vector review. I tested the Nitro Deck 2 for over a week, using it with both the Switch and Switch 2, as well as with a PC and my Android smartphone. I tested both wired and wireless connections. I also tested CRKD’s companion mobile app. I played games such as Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse, both of which are good tests for the responsiveness of the buttons and comfort of the D-pad. I also played The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom, which is a great test of all facets of a controller, including the motion controls. I’ve been gaming for decades and have plenty of experience testing controllers and other peripherals for numerous platforms, including the Switch and Switch 2. I’ve also reviewed other Switch 2 accessories, including handheld grips.

item.title: REVIEW: JMGO N3 Ultimate Review: This 4K Projector Is a Bright Gimbal Giant
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The JMGO N3 Ultimate ($2,999) fits squarely in the category of high-end room-to-room portable projectors, a group that includes two of our Editors' Choice picks—the Hisense C2 Ultra and the Anker Nebula X1—as well as the Xgimi Horizon 20 Max. All four of these models offer high brightness, more-than-acceptable image quality, and robust built-in speakers. As with the Horizon 20 Max, the JMGO entry doesn't offer quite enough to earn our Editors' Choice award, but it's a highly capable contender. The N3 Ultimate shares the same basic design as the other three models mentioned here. The projector itself is a near cube permanently attached to a gimbal mount. Point it straight ahead so it's parallel to the ground, and the overall dimensions are 10.8 by 12.1 by 9 inches (HWD), making it the largest room-to-room model I've seen so far. It's also the heaviest, to the point where it's better described as luggable, at 15.3 pounds. A nice touch is that it comes packed in a foam carrying case that adds a handle, which helps improve its portability somewhat. As with nearly all current 4K room-to-room projectors, the N3 Ultimate uses a 1,920-by-1,080-pixel DLP chip and TI's fast-switch pixel shifting to put a 3,840-by-2,160-pixel image on the screen. As with many—including the three other models mentioned above—it pairs the chip with a tri-color laser engine. It even shares the same rating as the others for the color gamut: 110% of BT.2020 (aka Rec.2020), the standard for 4K UHD TVs. The rated lifetime for the light source is 25,000 hours. Setup for Google TV is standard, with Wi-Fi as the only option for connecting to your network. Two HDMI ports let you connect video sources, and a USB 3.0 port lets you read files from a USB key. The hardest part of the physical setup is deciding where to put the projector—you could install it almost anywhere. Between the gimbal mount and the menus, the N3 Ultimate offers every option for focusing and positioning the image I've ever seen, plus a few new ones. For adjusting image size, you can take advantage of a powered optical zoom that offers a throw ratio range of 0.88:1 to 1.7:1—that's nearly short-throw territory. The control also seamlessly and automatically switches to a digital zoom if you need to make the image even smaller. For adjusting position, the gimbals let you tilt the projector over a range of 150 degrees, from just below straight down to a few degrees beyond straight up, and rotate it 360 degrees horizontally. In addition to tilting and swiveling manually with just the right amount of resistance to stop the projector where you want it, the gimbals are also powered, so you can control the position with the remote. The menu offers a full set of the most common automatic setup features: autofocus, auto-keystone adjustment, obstacle avoidance, and screen fitting. It also adds AI image positioning, which determines the best image size and position on its own. As part of its process, the powered gimbal moves the image around in the general direction the projector's already facing, stopping the movement several times in the process before continuing, and adjusting the image size several times as well. If you don't agree with its final choices, you can then use any of the other options to adjust the size and position yourself. For those who would rather ignore all digital adjustments to maintain the highest available brightness and image quality, you can simply point the projector straight ahead, adjust the image size using optical zoom only, and use the projector's lens shift to move the image up, down, left, or right without any keystone distortion, which is what I did for my viewing tests. JMGO's website shows the lens shift as +/- 130% vertically and +/-53% horizontally, using a convention for measurement that's common among projector manufacturers, but misleading. I measured it at just half that, which is still substantial. A 130% total vertical shift means you can move the image more than a full screen height vertically, while the 53% total horizontal shift lets you move it about half its screen width horizontally, all without causing keystone distortion. The audio system is built around two 12.5-watt speakers, which deliver usable sound at high enough volume to fill a large family room. That said, the audio isn't as high-quality or as high-volume as some of its competition, which means you're more likely to want to add an external sound system. Connection options are limited to Bluetooth and the HDMI port that supports eARC. You can also set it to Bluetooth speaker mode to connect to it from another source. JMGO rates the projector's brightness at 5,800 ISO lumens (equivalent to ANSI lumens). But the only picture mode that comes close to being that bright also has a notably green bias and ramps up the fan noise to a level that almost anyone will consider intolerable. The good news is that the rest of the modes still qualify the N3 Ultimate as a bright projector. The one I picked as having the best image quality offered the level of image brightness that I expect from about 3,000 lumens. The menus include a Light Brightness setting, which adjusts image brightness (and laser power) in 10 steps. Even at the lowest setting, the image easily lit up the 90-inch screen I usually use for testing in a dark room, leading me to switch to a 130-inch screen. At full brightness, I could still lower the setting and have a suitably bright picture, but when using the highest setting, I found the image still comfortable for viewing in a dark room while also being suitably bright for SDR, HDR, and 3D—even with all the lights on in my test area. To wash out the image at all, I had to aim a floor lamp directly at the screen from about 12 feet away, and even then, the image was still watchable. For SDR, HDR10, and HLG input, the N3 Ultimate's menus offer eight predefined picture modes. The list of names is the same in each case, but the settings are saved separately, so you can pick the same mode name for all three kinds of input, adjust each version differently, and not have to readjust the settings every time the input mode changes. Each picture mode offers essentially the same rich set of options, except for AI-enhanced, which locks you out of some settings (including local contrast and color tuner), presumably because the AI logic is handling those. Adding still more options is that one of the picture modes—CineTuner Master—has a separate menu of its own with predefined color modes for different kinds of movies—including Romance & Drama, Thriller and Mystery, and Action Film—and it also lets you create more. When you pick CineTuner Master as the picture mode to use, you get the settings for whichever option is currently chosen on the CineTuner menu. Each CineTuner definition offers most of the same settings as the picture modes, so you can modify them while looking at the effect of each change on a sample image. As shipped, each mode offers distinctly different color for the image than most of the others. Together with their names, that suggests they're designed to let you pick the colors you like best, depending on the movie, in direct contradiction to the argument that you ought to try for accurate color reproduction, to match the colors the director intended. Which viewing philosophy you prefer is up to you, of course. But for my viewing tests, as well as for viewing for my own enjoyment, I always consider better color accuracy as a key reason to pick one mode over another. For 1080p SDR viewing, most of the modes are in the range of good enough or better by most people's standards. I settled on Soft mode, primarily because it had the most accurate color. The only change I made from the defaults was to turn off frame interpolation (labeled MEMC on the menus), because even at the low setting, it introduced an obvious digital video effect, making filmed material look like live video. After that one change, Soft mode handled our entire SDR test suite without problems. Colors were suitably accurate and nicely saturated, and the image offered good contrast across the board from dark to bright scenes, along with impressively good shadow detail and a sense of three-dimensionality in dark scenes. For 4K HDR10 input, I picked Movie mode as having the best color quality. Here again, I turned off frame interpolation, but I also made a few additional changes. With default settings, scenes dominated by midtones were a little darker than they should be. I was able to counter that by adjusting the Adaptive Luma, Local Contrast, and Gamma settings to brighten up the scenes, and I also raised the sharpness setting a bit. After my changes, Image quality for HDR earned the same general description as for SDR, but was better enough to notice a small improvement. I also saw essentially the same image quality with ad hoc testing using streaming material for Dolby Vision and HLG input. However, not having the same clips to look at as for our formal tests means I can't make a direct comparison. Note that Dolby Vision offers only two picture modes: Dolby Vision Dark and Dolby Vision Bright. The N3 Ultimate also supports 3D (at full HD resolution) in three formats: side-by-side, top-bottom, and Blu-ray 3D. However, it doesn't automatically switch to 3D. When I tested using a 3D Blu-ray disc, I had to go to the 3D menu and pick the appropriate setting. One welcome touch is that the menus offer all the same picture modes for 3D as for 2D. Also welcome is that I didn't see any crosstalk in my tests, and 3D-related motion artifacts were less obvious than typical in current 3D models. Rainbow artifacts (red/green/blue flashes) in my tests showed up often enough and lasted long enough that if you're sensitive to them, as I am, you may find them annoying. However, I didn't see any of the speckling that tri-color laser models can show. That said, how easily you see either issue varies from person to person—as well as with room lighting and screen material—and I tend to see rainbows much more easily than I see speckle. As with any projector that can show either issue, if you're concerned about it, be sure to buy from a source that allows easy returns without a restocking fee, so you can judge the projector yourself. Gamers will appreciate that the N3 Ultimate supports variable refresh rate (VRR) for smoother video performance and low input lag. However, the actual performance for input lag is a little mixed. Very much on the plus side, I measured it with my Bodnar 4K Lag Tester at 9.6 milliseconds (ms) for both 4K/60Hz and 1080p/60Hz input, 5.3ms for 1080p/120Hz input, and 2.7ms for 240Hz. On the other hand, the lag sometimes failed to drop to those short times, as it's supposed to, when I changed the lag setting from Normal to Extreme. I found that when that happened, I could get the projector to actually switch to Extreme by toggling the setting back and forth two or three times. But because the reading from my lag tester was the only indication that it hadn't changed, you'd have no way to know when you'd have to do that if you were using the projector for gaming. At this writing, JMGO is looking into the issue. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. All four projectors mentioned here are solid choices for a high-brightness, room-to-room portable 4K projector. But deciding among them isn't actually as difficult as it would seem, since their differences make it easy to choose the right one for your needs. If your main concern is top-tier image quality, take a close look at the Hisense C2 Ultra and the Anker Nebula X1, both of which excel in that regard. Between them, the C2 Ultra is less expensive—in fact, it's the least expensive in the group—while the X1 offers what's potentially the best audio system of the four, thanks in large part to its optional external speakers. The Horizon 20 Max and JMGO N3 Ultimate come in a close second to the first two models in terms of image quality. They're essentially tied on that score, as well as on features ranging from short input lag to powered lens shifts, with list prices only $80 apart. In fact, they're so similar that I even ran into problems with both trying to set them properly for input-lag testing. If you're interested in either, you might want to choose based solely on which is selling for less on the day you're ready to buy. Most of my current work for PCMag is about printers and projectors, but I've covered a wide variety of other subjects—in more than 4,000 pieces, over more than 40 years—including both computer-related areas and others ranging from ape language experiments, to politics, to cosmology, to space colonies. I've written for PCMag.com from its start, and for PC Magazine before that, as a Contributor, then a Contributing Editor, then as the Lead Analyst for Printers, Scanners, and Projectors, and now, after a short hiatus, back to Contributing Editor. I'm pretty sure I'm the only person who worked on every "Project Printer" blockbuster PCMag ever produced, often writing 15 or more reviews for the year's big printer blowout. (I snuck in a single review one year when I was writing a book, strictly so I could keep that claim alive.) I've always worked for PCMag as a freelancer, which has freed me to take time away to write nine books, be a major contributor to four others, and write for other publications, including Wired, Computer Shopper, Projector Central, and Science Digest, where I was Computers Editor. I also wrote a computer column at one point for The Newark Star-Ledger. Although I started my career primarily as a science (mostly physics and astronomy) and science-fiction writer (published in Analog), my non-computer-related work runs the gamut from the Project Data Book for NASA's Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite (written for GE's Astro-Space Division) to the script for a video overview of a top company in the gaming industry (that would be gambling, not video games). My books include The Underground Guide to Color Printers (Addison-Wesley), Troubleshooting Your PC (Microsoft Press), and Faster, Smarter Digital Photography (Microsoft Press). Having covered a wide range of subjects, I've developed a serial expertise in many of them. The ones most relevant to my current work at PCMag.com are all imaging technologies.

item.title: REVIEW: Vivo X500 Pro Max first impressions: Vivo came to play, and the competition should be nervous
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
Vivo could have played it safe with the X500 series. Give the phones a slightly faster processor, slap on a new coat of paint, throw around a few AI buzzwords, and call it a day. Nobody would have been particularly surprised. Thankfully, Vivo seems to have had other ideas. The new X500 lineup consists of three phones: the X500, X500 Pro, and X500 Pro Max. But don’t let the names fool you into thinking these are simply three sizes of the same phone. Each model has its own identity, with differences in display size, processing power, and camera hardware. The X500 gets a 6.59-inch display and the Dimensity 9600M, while the compact X500 Pro packs a 6.36-inch screen and the flagship Dimensity 9600 Pro. Then there’s the X500 Pro Max, the big boss of the family, with a larger display, upgraded cameras, and the same flagship silicon. I’ve got the Vivo X500 Pro Max in my hands, and there’s already plenty to get excited about. One important caveat, though: this is the global version, not the Chinese variant. The global launch is coming soon, so we’ll have to wait a little longer to see what the entire family brings to the table. For now, let’s talk about the phone that has caught my attention. Design and build: Subtle flex, maximum effect I’ve got the gray version, and honestly, this is the one I’d pick. The rear panel doesn’t scream for attention, but look a little closer, and there’s more going on than meets the eye. The lower half of the back has a matte finish sprinkled with tiny star-like details that shimmer when the light hits them. The upper half gets a slightly raised section with a different texture, although the entire surface remains smooth to the touch. It’s understated, classy, and just flashy enough to remind you that this isn’t some run-of-the-mill slab of glass. The camera island is still massive, because apparently smartphone manufacturers have collectively decided that subtle camera bumps are a thing of the past. At least Vivo has dressed it up with a color-matched ring, while the flash has switched from a line-shaped design to a circular one. Elsewhere, it’s business as usual, and that’s not a complaint. You get flat glass on the back, flat aluminum rails, and a flat display. The phone also retains its IP69 dust and water resistance rating, so a little rain shouldn’t send you into panic mode. The box includes a case, a USB cable, and a 90W charging adapter. Vivo also continues to offer an optional Photographer Kit with a shoulder strap, an extra quick-release hook, and a case featuring a camera control grip. There’s one accessory I wish the global version had borrowed from its Chinese sibling: a second case designed around the newer rear display, which lets you control the rear cameras when taking selfies. Because if you’re going to take selfies, why not use the better cameras? Sadly, global buyers miss out on this particular party trick. The X500 Pro Max gets a 6.85-inch AMOLED display, up from 6.78 inches on last year’s model. That’s bigger than the screen on the X300 Ultra, too. The resolution also matches the Ultra, giving the Pro Max a welcome bump over its predecessor. Peak brightness remains at an impressive 4,500 nits, while LTPO technology allows the refresh rate to adapt to what’s happening on the screen. This time, it can climb all the way to 144Hz. Translation: scrolling should feel ridiculously smooth, and animations should look slick. You also get an always-on display that can stay enabled permanently, an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor, USB 3.2 connectivity, dual stereo speakers, and four microphones. There’s still no dedicated camera button, but I can’t say I’m losing sleep over it. The customizable shortcut key is sticking around, and I’d much rather have a button I can configure to do what I want than another piece of hardware I might barely use. Performance: Two nanometers of trouble for the competition Here’s where things get properly interesting. The X500 Pro Max is the first phone to run MediaTek’s new 2nm Dimensity 9600 Pro chipset. Yes, two nanometers. We’re now at the point where smartphone processors sound like they belong in a physics lecture. The chip uses ARM’s latest CPU and GPU designs, with two ultra-prime cores clocked at 4.55GHz, three performance cores at 4.35GHz, and three additional cores at 3.1GHz. MediaTek also claims a 27% improvement in peak GPU performance. That’s a promising combination of raw power and improved efficiency, particularly for demanding games, intensive multitasking, and AI workloads. The chipset also supports LPDDR6 RAM and UFS 5 storage, although Vivo hasn’t confirmed whether the tested phone uses those newer standards or sticks with LPDDR5X memory and UFS 4.1 storage. We will talk more in depth in our full review. On the software front, OriginOS 7 runs on Android 17. OriginOS 6 was a significant step forward, so the latest version feels more like a refinement than a complete overhaul. The interface remains slick, and Vivo has added AI features, fluid motion, seamless interaction, and a new Snap Up Engine for system optimization. I’m not complaining about the familiar look. If something works this well, there’s no need to tear it apart just to make the update feel important. I’ll save the final verdict on performance for the full review. Cameras: The Ultra’s zoom, minus some of its bragging rights Vivo has refreshed almost the entire camera system, and the periscope telephoto camera is the star of the show. It’s the same unit found in the X300 Ultra, which is excellent news for anyone who enjoys zooming in without turning their photos into impressionist paintings. Honestly, the Vivo X500 Pro Max isn’t just chasing megapixels. It’s bringing some serious camera technology to the party, starting with one of Sony’s latest 50MP, 1/1.28-inch LOFIC CMOS image sensors. And no, LOFIC isn’t just another acronym for a marketing department to get excited about. Short for Lateral Overflow Integration Capacitor, LOFIC technology promises high dynamic range (HDR) images with less processing overhead. Instead of capturing multiple frames and stitching them together to preserve highlights, shadows, and details while controlling noise, the sensor can achieve similar results with a single shot. For content creators, that’s a pretty big deal. Moving subjects are less likely to end up looking like accidental double exposures, thanks to a reduced risk of ghosting. The technology also enables more efficient HDR 4K video recording at 60 frames per second while lowering power consumption. Your footage gets the upgrade, without your battery necessarily paying the price. The camera hardware doesn’t stop there. The X500 Pro Max retains a 200MP telephoto camera and a 50MP ultrawide shooter, complementing the new main sensor. Features such as 4K Cinematic Colour Video, Auto-framing, and Stage Mode 3.0 further position this phone as a serious tool for creators rather than just another expensive rectangle for social media scrolling. Want to get closer to distant subjects? Vivo also offers optional 200mm and 400mm telephoto extender lenses, much like those available for the X300 Ultra. These accessories open up additional possibilities for long-range photography and creative framing. Just remember that they’re sold separately, because apparently getting closer to your subject comes with an additional price tag. But no, the X500 Pro Max doesn’t steal every advantage from its Ultra sibling. But with upgrades to every camera except the selfie shooter, Vivo clearly hasn’t treated photography as an afterthought. Thankfully, the cameras appear to be where Vivo wants to make the biggest noise. First impressions: This is how you do an annual upgrade The biggest surprise about the Vivo X500 Pro Max is just how much Vivo has changed. A larger display, a new 2nm flagship chipset, refreshed cameras, and a massive battery are not the sort of upgrades I’d dismiss as incremental. The Chinese version gets an 8,000mAh battery, while the global model, which is our unit, comes in at 7,800mAh. That’s a serious amount of battery for a flagship, especially when paired with a chip designed to improve efficiency. Wired charging remains at 90W, with 40W wireless charging for those who prefer to ditch the cable. Of course, impressive specifications don’t automatically make a great phone. I still need to test battery endurance, sustained performance, camera consistency, and how well the software holds up during everyday use. I went into the Vivo X500 Pro Max expecting a decent flagship refresh. Instead, Vivo seems determined to make the competition work a little harder. A massive 7,800mAh battery, a 2nm flagship chipset, a sharper 144Hz display, and meaningful camera upgrades make this feel like more than a yearly exercise in changing numbers on a spec sheet. The camera system is particularly intriguing. With a new Sony 50MP LOFIC main sensor designed to capture HDR images in a single shot, a 200MP periscope telephoto camera, and a 50MP ultrawide shooter, Vivo appears to be taking mobile photography seriously. The promise of reduced subject ghosting and more efficient HDR 4K video recording at 60fps could make this an especially compelling option for content creators. Add support for optional telephoto extender lenses, and the X500 Pro Max starts looking like a rather capable camera that happens to make phone calls. Of course, the real test is still ahead. Battery endurance, sustained performance, and camera consistency will determine whether the X500 Pro Max is genuinely great or simply looks impressive on paper. But Vivo has already given me plenty of reasons to be optimistic. The X500 Pro Max doesn’t look like a phone that exists merely to justify a new number on the box. It looks like Vivo actually sat down, identified what mattered, and decided to do something about it. If the full review backs up these early impressions, Vivo might have a serious flagship contender on its hands. And if other smartphone makers are watching, here’s a friendly suggestion: take notes. Also, in the meantime, here’s our Vivo X300 Ultra review.

item.title: REVIEW: The Boox Palma 2 Pro finally got me to stop reading on my phone
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch
The $400 Boox Palma 2 Pro is a smartphone-sized e-reader designed for people who want to read books, articles, and documents on a small E Ink display. However, it offers more than just a dedicated reading experience because it runs Android and supports Google Play, giving you access to third-party apps. Think of it as a cross between a Kindle and a compact Android tablet. What drew me to reviewing the Palma 2 Pro was its size. When I’m not reading a physical book, I like to lie on my side and read at night before bed. Most e-readers are squarish and hard to hold without something like a PopSocket, and they can feel too big for reading while lying down. So even though I own a Kindle, I often ended up reading on my iPhone simply because it was more comfortable in my hand. But, reading on your phone for too long can of course cause eye strain. The Palma 2 Pro ultimately solved this problem for me during the two months I spent testing it. The device’s front-lit screen lets you choose between cool and warm lighting. This was a big plus for me because when I’m reading in bed at night, I don’t want to disturb my sleeping husband with the light. While you can lower the brightness on a smartphone, the Palma 2 Pro can be dimmed to an exceptionally low level. Even when reading in complete darkness, I could see the screen clearly without straining my eyes or disturbing my husband. Not only was the Boox Palma 2 Pro easier on my eyes, but it was also noticeably lighter than my iPhone, weighing just 175 grams and making it even more comfortable to hold. And since it’s pocket-sized, I ended up carrying it everywhere, from the doctor’s office to the airport, especially since it fits in my small, everyday purse that isn’t big enough for a Kindle. So, in moments when I would normally scroll on my phone, I was getting some reading in instead. Since it’s not a locked-down e-reader, you can download apps like Kindle, Kobo, and Libby, as well as apps for audiobooks, podcasts, read-it-later services, and email. This means that you don’t have to use the built-in reader app, and can choose to read on your preferred app. Access to apps turns the compact E Ink device into a versatile tool for reading, research, and productivity. It’s worth noting that while scrolling through these apps, animations and some interfaces may feel sluggish because not all apps are optimized for E Ink. And while the device is capable of displaying color, images will definitely look less vibrant than they would a smartphone screen. For me, the Palma 2 Pro became a dedicated device for reading and listening to audiobooks, which allowed me to enjoy the best of both worlds without the usual distractions that come with a smartphone. The Boox Palma 2 Pro also features a rear camera for scanning documents, a built-in speaker for listening to audio without headphones, and a hybrid SIM slot for cellular data on the go. The device is compatible with a stylus, so you can take notes and mark up PDFs. However, I can’t speak to that experience since I didn’t receive a stylus with my review unit. As for battery life, the device lasted about 5–7 days, which worked for me but could be a downside for people who are used to Kindles, which can last for weeks on a single charge. Additionally, if you want to get more juice out of the device, you can just turn off Wi-Fi. One downside I found, especially for an e-reader at this price point, is that there’s quite a bit of ghosting. Text from a previous page can linger on the screen when you turn to the next page or return to the home screen. There’s a refresh button in the navigation bar that quickly clears it, but it may get annoying for some users to repeatedly have to do that. I think the Boox Palma 2 Pro is a great device for a very specific type of reader: someone who wants a smartphone-sized device for comfort, portability, as well as access to apps. If you’re someone who loves your Kindle, I don’t think this device is for you. But if, like me, you’re tired of reading on your phone and dealing with eye strain or headaches, the Boox Palma 2 Pro is a great option. Of course, the price is quite steep for an e-reader, so you’ll have to decide whether the added versatility and portability are worth the extra cost. It’s worth mentioning that Boox is launching a non-Pro Palma 3 soon for $340 that features a black and white display and replaces the Palma 2.

item.title: REVIEW: CMF Clip Pro Review: Open Earbuds With an Inspired Design and a Few Quirks
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The CMF Clip Pro ($99) fuses Nothing’s knack for style and sound quality into a pair of open earbuds, which are safer to listen to while you’re out and about. A useful special case and have surprisingly good mics set these buds apart somewhat, although they aren't as competitively priced as some of Nothing’s other recent audio forays. The Clip Pro costs more than our Editors’ Choice open clip-style earbuds, the Earfun Clip 2 ($79.99), while providing less subbass and fewer sound customization options. The Earfun Clip 2 buds remain the more sensible buy for most people. Like many other products from Nothing, the CMF Clip Pro earbuds have a unique design with a curious emphasis on asymmetry and a two-tone color scheme. It makes them distinct. The case is fun-looking, but a little bulky. This lets it incorporate the buds and a unique rotary dial that essentially provides extra remote control over the buds. The case feels sturdy enough, but the dial’s attachment wiggles enough to feel flimsy. To Nothing’s credit, the case gets IPX2 ingress protection, so a drop of rain now and then shouldn’t kill it. Flipping the case open reveals the buds, which also sit in an unusual fashion—slightly off-axis to the width of the case and running slightly parallel, but not in line with one another. It’s a smart enough way to squeeze them in efficiently while furthering the distinctive aesthetic the brand goes for. The buds themselves feature a single color on the linking arm and a different color on the battery and driver housings. Those two housings are also different shapes, with one spherical and the other cylindrical. The design seems more aesthetically minded than ergonomic, as the cylinder feels a little odd on the back of my ear, and the sphere doesn’t do much to ensure optical orientation toward my ear canal. Although I didn’t have any issues with the buds staying on my ears, they never felt entirely secure. The linkage wrapping around my ears is quite flexible, which made it a bit too easy to unseat the buds with a light brush during testing. This does avoid a strong clamping on the ears at least, so comfort is a plus here. The buds are also light at about 0.21 ounces apiece, so I never feel their weight on my ears. Sometimes, after I’ve worn them for a while and then removed them, I feel like they might still be there because their presence is so subtle. The many seams on the buds raise quality-control concerns. The gaps between elements aren’t consistent, which makes the buds look seem cheaply put together. Nothing happened to send two pairs for testing, which was a stroke of luck, as one had its left driver distort heavily and consistently on one of our test tracks, despite exhibiting no issues over hours of listening beforehand. The second pair performed flawlessly throughout testing. Nothing rates the buds to IP54, so they should at least keep a good deal of dust and water out, but the quality issues have me wondering how long that protection will hold up. The buds pack 10.8mm drivers and have a fairly large grille that helps ensure sound reaches the ear canal, even if the buds don't fit the same in everyone's ears. Playback won’t be perfectly consistent from fit to fit, though. The buds claim to support a frequency response range from 20Hz to 40kHz, though, as I’ll delve into later, that lower figure is a stretch. The buds connect to devices over Bluetooth 5.4 and support LDAC, AAC, and SBC as a fallback. They can pair with two devices at a time using Multipoint, and I found they switch back and forth without any fuss. Connecting to Android and Windows devices is quick with Google Fast Pair and Microsoft Swift Pair. Despite the connectivity options, I found their connection could be a little spotty in motion, particularly if I turned my head quickly, which undermines their utility outdoors, where you’ll be more likely to look around frequently. On-ear controls consist of a button at the end of the cylindrical portion of each bud that’s easy to feel out and consistent to press. The buds respond to single-, double-, triple-, and long-presses as well as a double-press-and-hold control. The single-press cannot be modified. But the remaining controls are customizable, with options to adjust the left and right earbud controls independently. The case essentially offers redundant controls. By default, the dial does nothing other than serve as the pairing button. It takes the same input controls as the earbud, but can also rotate to adjust volume. The double-press-and-hold control is the only one that can’t be customized here, and it’s locked to disabling/enabling the dial itself. Having experienced the dial adjust the volume on its own while the case was in my pocket, a disable option seems smart. The Clip Pro buds are rated to run for a lengthy 10 hours, and they’ve lived up to that claim in testing, holding up even over the course of a long work day. LDAC will likely take a large chunk of that battery life, but since these aren't buds meant for focused music listening, AAC is what most people should stick with. The charging case, despite its size, only brings 22.5 extra hours of charge to raise the total battery life to 32.5 hours, which is a ways shy of the EarFun Clip 2 buds’ 40 hours. Annoyingly, when the charging case is fully discharged, the buds no longer seem to respond to insertion, so they’ll remain on and connected to your phone or laptop even after you put them away unless you manually disconnect them. The buds recharge quickly, with 10 minutes of charging giving them four hours of playback time. The case has a USB-C port on the back, and Nothing includes a USB-C cable for the job. You don’t get wireless charging here, though. The Clip Pro works with the Nothing X app that manages the company's other accessories, such as the Nothing Ear 3a or Headphone a, and no account is required to use it. It’s a stylish app that lays out info and settings in an easily-navigable tile format. While not everything is fully described at first, most settings are just a click away from a clear description of their behavior. The app includes a spatial audio mode that tries to make audio sound like it’s coming from all around you. It’s not entirely unsuccessful, but it sounds a bit too echoey and cuppy for me to use often. There’s also an anti-leakage mode that lowers volume and shifts the EQ automatically to reduce how much sound slips out of your ears. It may be good for privacy, but it’s bad for audio quality. You can set it to automatically activate only for calls, leave it running all the time, or disable it completely. EQ control is broken up into two areas. A dedicated bass enhancement boosts it considerably with three level options. Then there’s a simple equalizer with five genre presets, and a not-so-comprehensive custom option with only three sliders and 6dB of adjustment in either direction. By default, the buds use the Pop EQ setting and max Bass Enhancement. The Clip Pro also has toggles for Multipoint connections and a low-lag mode, though I found the latency sufficiently low for watching videos with clean lip-syncing even without it. A control in the Multipoint menu to begin pairing would have been convenient instead of having to place the buds back in the case and manually pair with your second device. In the device settings menu within the app, you’ll find the option to enable LDAC, a “Long battery life mode” that uses AAC and reduces bass levels to extend the battery life (albeit only to 36 hours total), and an earbud finder tool that emits a loud noise so you can hear dropped buds. The Clip Pro buds aren’t the ultimate package in terms of audio quality, but they do a decent job. Perhaps more importantly, they can pump out quite a bit of sound while still providing transparency, so you can hear what you’re listening to and your surroundings. I found the sound more than sufficient for podcasts and music while out running. In The Knife’s “Silent Shout,” the buds show their knack for upbeat, energetic sound. They pump out the bass triplets and even groove on the sub-bass quarter notes. They keep those triplets and quarter notes tight, though partly as a result of a lack of depth that leaves some of the notes subdued. The synth melody is poignant through the buds, but the upper vocal harmony and some of the upper-register atmospheric instruments are slightly buried. Kendrick Lamar’s “Loyalty” highlights some shortcomings of the Clip Pro. The deep sub-bass line introduced in the first chorus is too low for the buds to reproduce with much volume. Even with the maximum Bass Enhancement that the buds default to, few of the lowest notes come through in the mix, while the highest of the line leaps up in volume because it falls further into the buds’ effective range. The drums don’t get the lifelike feel from the buds' higher playback quality; cymbals in particular lack sizzle. Enabling LDAC restores some high-frequency detail but can affect battery life. Bill Callahan’s “Drover” especially benefits from the extra detail LDAC can bring. The guitars and fiddle sound a lot more lifelike with the extra texture. Callahan’s baritone vocals are slightly subdued, not getting the full-bodied sound they can from superior headphones, but they’re at least mostly clear. The mellow bass keeps the drums from becoming overpowering. The Clip Pro is a poor match for orchestral music like John Adams’ The Gospel According to the Other Mary. The weak low-end response drains some instruments of their heft. And the need to blend all the sound together right before the ear canal can make the more complex instrumentation sound more sloppy than precise. One important detail regarding sound quality stems from fit and ear shape. The Clip Pro buds sit inside the ear opening and clip around the back, but this will make their fit vary considerably from ear to ear. Subtle shifts in positioning can thin out the mids and high-end or boost the bass. Some buds, like the EarFun Clip 2, felt like they consistently landed in the same spot when I wore them, producing a more consistent sound from one day to the next, but the Clip Pro buds haven’t felt as secure or consistent. The mics are surprisingly competent. Whether in a quiet, tame environment or a noisier one, they do a good job of isolating my voice. I sound decently full through the buds, though it sounds a bit like it is passing through cardboard. It may not be high enough quality to field calls all day or to make a podcast, but it passes muster for regular hands-free calling. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The CMF Clip Pro buds have style, though there are some cracks in the seams when you look close (literally). They don’t seem feel as polished as they could have been, but their funky looks help distract from that at least. They offer punchy sound that’s easy to hear while keeping abreast of your surroundings, even if the sound isn’t quite as refined as some of Nothing’s other products. Ultimately, these $99 buds can't quite compete with the EarFun Clip 2, which I found fit more securely, sounded better, had longer battery life, and cost less, helping them maintain their Editors’ Choice ranking for open earbuds.
